item.title: Unusual bird spotted on Guam ahead of Typhoon Champi
item.description: A day before Typhoon Champi put Guam in Condition of Readiness 1, what Jessica Laguaña mistook for a chicken ended up being a rare sighting of an Australasian swamphen. Laguaña was driving in Ordot to check on her in-laws when she noticed the bird near their driveway. Its striking blue-purple feathers caught her attention, prompting her to take a photo.
item.content:encoded:
A day before Typhoon Champi put Guam in Condition of Readiness 1, what Jessica Laguaña mistook for a chicken ended up being a rare sighting of an Australasian swamphen.

Laguaña was driving in Ordot to check on her in-laws when she noticed the bird near their driveway. Its striking blue-purple feathers caught her attention, prompting her to take a photo.

“I was so captivated by the blue on its chest. The bird was coming up the driveway, and it seemed like it wasn’t afraid of me. I walked by it, and it just kept going up the driveway.” Laguaña said her father-in-law leaves bird feed for the local birds in the area, and that it might have been around the area before. She said her father-in-law had seen the bird a few times prior to Typhoon Champi.

The bird’s bright red bill and oversized red frontal shield also distinguish it from Guam’s pulattat bird, or common morehen.

Avian biologist Martin Kastner said the bird can be confidently identified as the Australasian swamphen, although a similar-looking black-backed swamphen cannot be ruled out completely.

Swamphens are generally sedentary, but can disperse between islands. Kastner said the bird’s appearance on Guam is unusual, and it remains unclear whether more will be seen.

“So if this is the only bird on island, which is possible, then we might not see them very often, and it could be a one-off,” Kastner said.

Guam has no known subfossil records of its own due to the cave damage on Guam during the war. However, swamphen subfossils have been found on Rota and Tinian, suggesting the birds may have once inhabited the Marianas.

The nearest population is in Palau, where a rare endemic subspecies known as the Uek lives in marshes and taro patches and its protected by local custom.

For now, the swamphen’s origins remain a mystery. Kastner said it will be interesting to see whether any more appear on Guam.

item.content:encoded:
Typhoon In-Fa remained on track to pass about 180 miles north of Saipan and about 300 miles north of Guam on Friday, according to the Joint Typhoon Warning Center.

On Tuesday afternoon, In-Fa was located at 14.3 degrees north latitude and 162.2 degrees east longitude, more than 1,100 miles east of Guam. It was a Category 3 storm with winds of 125 mph, and was moving to the west-northwest at 2 mph.

Forecasters with the National Weather Service said In-Fa was expected to make a slight turn toward the west and increase in forward speed through Wednesday, then turn back to the west-northwest.

The storm was expected to begin intensifying on Wednesday night.

Typhoon winds extended out 35 miles from the center of the storm, with tropical storm-force winds extending 90 miles from the center.

item.title: CNMI delegate urges path forward as DHS halts Chinese travel program

Kimberlyn King-Hinds said Tuesday she is working with federal officials to address concerns that prompted the suspension of a key travel program for Chinese visitors to the Northern Mariana Islands. item.content:encoded:
Emphasizing that the program has been "suspended, not terminated," CNMI Del. Kimberlyn King-Hinds said Tuesday she is working with federal officials to address concerns that prompted the suspension of a key travel program for Chinese visitors to the Northern Mariana Islands.

King-Hinds said she spoke directly with the White House, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and House leadership following the Department of Homeland Security's announcement suspending the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands Economic Vitality and Security Travel Authorization Program, or EVS-TAP. She said Mullin assured her that DHS would work directly with the CNMI to better understand and address the issues that led to the suspension.

King-HInds said, "We have experienced interruptions to travel programs serving the Commonwealth before, and we will work through this together with our federal partners to address the concerns that have been raised and find a path forward, just as we have done before."

According to the delegate, the program was established with safeguards allowing DHS to suspend operations when security or law enforcement concerns arise. She said federal and local officials would work together to address those concerns and support the program's resumption as quickly as possible.

The congresswoman also warned that a lengthy suspension could further burden the Commonwealth's struggling tourism sector.

"Our tourism industry is already facing tremendous challenges, and a prolonged disruption would have serious consequences for our businesses, workers and families," King-Hinds said. "We must also consider the immediate effects on airlines, travel arrangements, and the businesses that depend on visitor arrivals."

The Department of Homeland Security announced Tuesday that it will suspend EVS-TAP effective Oct. 30, requiring Chinese nationals seeking to visit the CNMI for business or tourism to obtain a U.S. visa unless another lawful exception applies.

Chinese nationals already admitted under the program may remain through their authorized period of stay.

In a Federal Register notice, DHS said the program's suspension was warranted because of national security, immigration enforcement and law enforcement concerns. The agency cited the risk of unauthorized travel beyond the CNMI, potential espionage activities involving sensitive military infrastructure in the Mariana Islands, birth tourism concerns and previous criminal cases involving the smuggling of Chinese nationals from the CNMI to Guam.

EVS-TAP took effect in February 2025 and allowed pre-screened nationals of the People's Republic of China to travel directly to the CNMI without first obtaining a U.S. visa. More than 3,000 Chinese nationals used the program during fiscal year 2025, according to DHS.

While acknowledging that some CNMI businesses have relied on Chinese tourism, DHS said economic considerations do not outweigh what it described as acute national security, immigration and law enforcement concerns. The agency noted that Chinese visitors may still travel to the CNMI through the standard U.S. visa process.

King-Hinds said her immediate focus is ensuring the concerns identified by federal officials are addressed so the program can resume.

item.content:encoded:
In the summer of 2020, I lived briefly in Ithaca, New York. It's the only time I've lived near Aldi, the grocery store known for low prices. I went twice, and I thought it was fine, but underwhelming. I appreciated the low prices, but it didn't have everything I needed. The store was small and a bit shabby.

I didn't know it yet, but those are the exact ingredients that have made Aldi the fastest-growing grocery chain in America. Per Bloomberg , Aldi plans to have more than 3,000 American locations by the end of 2028, which would be more than any other chain but Walmart. In 2024, Aldi generated some $29 billion in U.S. sales, which is more than Trader Joe's.

Aldi is a German company known for having low, low prices, and it deserves that reputation. Food reporter Deena Shanker told me that her experience comparison shopping over many months was that Aldi either matched Walmart on price or was a bit cheaper. Grocers like Wegmans and Kroger have announced defensive price reductions, and an analysis published in late 2023 of Lidl, another German grocer with a very similar model to Aldi's but fewer U.S. stores, found that grocery chains reduced their markups ~7 percent in areas where Lidl stores opened .

All to say: Aldi is disrupting the grocery business and actually lowering prices even as the cost of food—at restaurants and other grocery stores—goes up and up.

Maybe this sounds a bit humdrum. But I found it totally intriguing and perplexing, because…

One necessary but not sufficient explanation for Aldi's low prices is that management is obsessed with efficiency and cutting unnecessary costs. There's no music in stores, because speakers (and licensing fees for muzak) cost money. The staff places products on shelves still in the cardboard boxes they were trucked in on, because artfully unpacking fruits, bread, and jerky sticks would mean higher labor costs. The shabbiness is intentional — it's the cost of cheaper groceries.

But other grocery chains are similarly obsessed with efficiency. Here's one of my favorite examples about Costco, courtesy of Zachary Crockett and The Hustle : "In another instance, reengineering a container of cashews from a circle to a square shape allowed Costco to stack more items in a single truck, reducing the number of shipments by 24,000 pallets per year. For shoppers, this meant cheaper nuts."

Instead, Aldi's disruptively low prices rely on two primary tactics:

Aldi's low prices made their stores very attractive during periods like the Great Recession and today's inflationary era. The Great Recession, especially, enabled their current growth. But if all Aldi offered was bargain prices in shabby stores, customers might flee to Costco, Kroger, or Whole Foods when the economy recovered.

So another key to Aldi's success is that it's fun. Aldi has a famously chaotic-good middle aisle with rotating buys like fun toys, German spätzle, and advent calendars that contain 24 festive cheeses. And its U.S. stores have expanded their offerings (a bit) to attract higher-income customers: Aldi doesn't just have the cheapest apples, but the cheapest honey crisp apples. Not just super-duper cheap wine but well-priced "premium" wine.

Instead of being a sad place to shop when you're low on cash, Aldi has more flea-market energy: a place anyone might go to hunt for good deals and fun finds. Aldi is beloved; many customers are cult-like in their devotion . In some cases, customers line up for new store openings like early iPhone releases.

My main takeaway from researching and analyzing Aldi for several weeks (for an episode of Gastronomics !) is that there's always something new under the sun. American grocery stores are a mature market. They seem pretty stable equilibrium-y. But they are dynamic and always changing. Aldi didn't need futuristic tech to disrupt the industry; just a strategy developed 80 years ago, then tweaked for the American market. In healthy markets, there's always a way in for new competitors.

My other takeaway is greater appreciation for the famous business idiom: "There are only two ways to make money in business: One is to bundle; the other is to unbundle."

The clearest example of bundling and unbundling is probably television. Cable companies bundled hundreds of TV channels together and charged one high fee for all of them. Then streaming services like Netflix made money by unbundling television — by allowing people to pay for just Netflix. Which felt liberating! For a few years. But now customers are annoyed about subscribing to so many streaming services. So streamers are teaming up to form bundles, like getting Disney, Hulu, and HBO Max all for one reduced price. Now, to make money, you gotta bundle.

Even the person who coined the phrase about bundling and unbundling didn't think it's literally the only way to make money. Still, I often failed to see (un)bundling as a powerful framework outside of the media industry. Until I realized that Aldi is unbundling the grocery store.

For a long time, grocery stores got more bundled. People once went to the baker, the butcher, and the greengrocer. Then the super market put all those things under one roof. And then Walmart, Target, and Costco created superstores where you could buy groceries and clothes and big-screen TVs.

Now Aldi is reversing this process by unbundling the grocery store. Not only does Aldi not have the big-screen TVs and dupes of Lululemon hoodies and pants , it doesn't even have everything on your grocery list. Aldi unbundled the part of the grocery business it can do super cheaply, and it intentionally locates Aldi stores near competitor grocery stores so shoppers can easily go grab the last few things on their list (the rest of the bundle).

With this in mind, I've started seeing bundling and unbundling at work in more and more industries. If you look closely at your own, I suspect you will, too.

My third takeaway is that I just didn't live in Ithaca long enough to grok Aldi. If I'd been there longer, I bet I would have made Aldi part of a multi-store strategy. I get it now! Aldi, please come to Colorado (where I live)!

At the start of this post, I asked three questions inspired by Aldi's expansion. The first two, which are about how Aldi achieved a comparative advantage, I feel like I've answered.

The third was whether the American economy can still deliver a bounty of affordable food. I think the way Aldi's growth pressured competitors to keep prices low shows that grocers are not the right target of our ire over food prices. But grocery stores are just one slice of the food world.

item.title: Can Black voting power and Trump fatigue break Mississippi's red wall?
item.description: COLUMBUS, Miss. — On paper, Mississippi's U.S. Senate race seems like the perfect place for a political upset this year, an assertion President Trump's Monday rally there seems to support. item.content:encoded:
COLUMBUS, Miss. — On paper, Mississippi's U.S. Senate race seems like the perfect place for a political upset this year, an assertion President Trump's Monday rally there seems to support.

It has the highest share of Black voters in the country, at close to 40%. It's a rural, agriculture-heavy state that is also among the poorest, so higher prices are felt harder.

But President Trump won the state by 23 points in 2024, and it's extremely racially polarized, meaning not enough white voters back Democrats for the party to win statewide.

In a midterm environment that has seen hundreds of millions of dollars poured into Senate races in conservative-heavy states like Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Alaska, and a last-minute flood of cash to Kansas , the Magnolia state has been left off of many peoples' radar — and largely out of campaign investments.

Scott Colom, a district attorney and the Democratic Senate nominee in Mississippi, told NPR that's a mistake.

"The reality is, Mississippi has never been a lost cause, we've been a betrayed cause," he said. "The Democratic Party has not been trying to win Mississippi. Let's stop kidding ourselves, right? They spent hundreds of millions of dollars in other states. They spent almost nothing in Mississippi."

Colom is challenging incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, who blocked his nomination to be a federal judge during the Biden administration.

In the final weeks of the election, both parties have rushed to spend millions of dollars in Mississippi, as national polling shows a pathway where Democratic enthusiasm and elevated Black turnout, combined with fewer Republican base voters and defections from the party, has made deep red races deeply competitive this cycle.

At a rally for Colom in his hometown high school gym Thursday, about a thousand people showed up to hear the candidate — joined by former Vice President Kamala Harris — give his closing message.

Many attendees expressed optimism for his campaign coupled with a vibe of feeling down about those in power, regardless of party affiliation – citing the war in Iran, rising fuel costs and dissatisfaction with Trump's second term.

That includes Celestine Rice, who said many people were realizing a need to focus on bringing change to the political system and representation.

"Before, we didn't realize how bad it was, but now it's obvious," she said. "The moral compass of this country is gone."

Rice said many people took for granted an era where it seemed the country used to be more focused on taking care of its citizens and now they see that "big money, it doesn't trickle down like they said."

The brunt of the Democratic money and manpower headed to Mississippi is driven by a growing number of those who argue the party's future runs through the South, including Harris, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock and former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg.

At the rally, Harris said political changes in the last year and a half were the result of "the most callous, corrupt and incompetent presidential administration we have ever experienced."

"We've been going through that range of emotions from anger to sadness to depression, all of that for a year and a half," she said. "Well guess what? We're 12 days out from an election. And it's time to turn that anger into action."

About a hundred miles up the road a few days later, Trump, Hyde-Smith and other Mississippi Republicans gathered in Corinth to motivate the party's base to show up and vote next Tuesday.

In a statement ahead of the rally, Hyde-Smith's campaign manager expressed confidence in her reelection bid.

"We are confident that Mississippians will once again send Cindy Hyde-Smith to the U.S. Senate," Jake Monssen said. "Senator Hyde-Smith and President Trump have built a strong working relationship, and she gladly accepted when President Trump offered to help rally voters and support her get-out-the-vote efforts.

"With so much at stake in this election, Mississippians deserve to hear directly from their President about the consequences of electing Democrats, the radical socialist policies being pushed by Scott Colom, and the importance of this election. Team Cindy looks forward to a successful, high-energy event in Corinth," he said.

Speaking ahead of the president, Hyde-Smith touted accomplishments from her time in office and said the choice facing voters "could not be clearer."

"We know what we're looking at: this is socialism versus capitalism, and we know that," she said. "Communism versus democracy, and big government versus the free market. It could not be higher stakes."

Hyde-Smith repeatedly reiterated that it was important for Republicans to get out and vote.

"Endorsements don't win elections, votes win elections," she said.

For his part, Trump said his visit to Mississippi was because Hyde-Smith was in good shape in her matchup.

"Sometimes when you think somebody's doing so well, nobody votes," Trump said. "'Oh, Cindy's great, she's gonna do no problem, let's stay home.' And then bad things happen, Cindy. That's why I'm here, just get out and vote."

Over the last month, the Republican campaign strategy has been to highlight the investment and attention from national Democrats as proof Colom is too extreme for Mississippi — and have spent heavily on ads saying as much.

"Meet the most radical Senate candidate in our lifetime, Scott Colom," an ad titled "Most Radical" intones. "Twice nominated by Biden, beholden to the far left. As DA, violent crime doubled on his watch."

The Hyde-Smith campaign has spent more than $1.3 million on that ad, according to data from AdImpact.

But Democrats have spent more this month, about $5 million to the Republicans' $3.2 million, with a message that there's no daylight between the unpopular president and down ballot Republicans.

item.title: From ghostwriters to false identities: Our favorite fake music scandals of the 21st century

item.content:encoded:
From manufactured fans to AI artists and "industry plants," 2026 is one wild year for figuring out what's authentic and what's not in the music industry. For more, check out a catalog of the year in musical fraudulence, an essay by Ann Powers on where our desire for authenticity comes from and a conversation about why it feels harder than ever to know what's real in our podcast.

This year feels like an especially fraught time to bicker about authenticity in the music industry. Yes, we now have generative AI to contend with. Yes, every other week there seems to be a new artist zooming toward the top of the Billboard charts with such unprecedented speed and staying there, leading to skepticism about the promotional mechanisms behind them. From titanic pop stars to indie rock stars, everyone's clamoring for just a song's length worth of your precious attention span.

We're spending this week examining the factors that have converged to make 2026 feel like a new high-water mark in the flood of musical fraudulence. But as Ann Powers wrote in her essay, this feeling is hardly unique in music history — and it has only accelerated in the last few decades. As new technologies and new routes of music discovery have emerged, conspiracies and insecurities about the purity of music have always followed suit. Here, NPR Music staffers share their favorite fake music scandals from the 21st century.

At first, they tried authenticity. In 2001, Gavin Bain and Billy Boyd trekked from Dundee, Scotland to London for an open audition with Polydor Records, rapping in their native Scottish brogues, only to be laughed off and dismissed as "the rapping Proclaimers." So the pair regrouped and transfigured themselves into something they figured would be more desirable to a recording industry eager to replicate the meteoric success of Eminem: brash, white emcees from America.

The fabrication paid off. With their American accents perfected, Sony UK signed them as Silibil N' Brains, a duo hailing from Huntington Beach, Calif. They (the story went) had met at a rap battle in San Francisco. They skateboarded. They rapped with a nasally gang vocal reminiscent of the Beastie Boys. At their height, they opened for D12 at Brixton Academy. They kept up the guise for executives, managers, audiences and even girlfriends.

As the lie deepened, it took its toll on the pair. "Eventually, we couldn't come out of character," Bain told NPR in 2010 . From their perch in London, they called home less and less, finding it difficult to switch off the personas. "It was complete insanity."

Their drug use and drinking accelerated, Bain told NPR, and he and Boyd began fighting. Then, in June 2005 , a blowup row broke the band, and Boyd went back to Scotland. They had pretended to be American for two years, and Bain would continue the ruse for another two, trying to launch a solo career before finally breaking character in a dramatic onstage reveal in 2007.

In the years since, Bain and Boyd have publicly wrestled with each other over what exactly happened, adding a fittingly muddled layer to any authoritative account of Silibil N' Brains. "There's so much lies about the lies about the lies," Boyd said in the 2013 documentary The Great Hip Hop Hoax . And the mythology continues to grow: A James McAvoy-directed feature film about the duo based on Bain's 2010 memoir was just released in the U.S. "I think Gavin is still chasing something, still looking for his identity in that. And that's great for him — it's a great marketing ploy," Boyd told a British newspaper earlier this year.

Would Silibil N' Brains have been able to hoodwink the recording industry today? The pair blew up in an era before extensive digital footprints could have easily revealed their true identities. But something at the heart of their story feels eternal: fabricated authenticity can beat the real thing if it gives the industry what it wants. — Noah Caldwell

Even within the perceived "goody two-shoes" world of classical music, dark secrets can lurk.

Consider the story of Joyce Hatto, the English pianist whose career began unremarkably in the 1950s and ended in one of the strangest scandals in the history of recordings.

Hatto grew up in a music-loving family, where her father was a piano enthusiast. She later claimed she had studied with the legendary Alfred Cortot. Her talent, by many accounts of the day, was middling. Still, over a 25-year period, she gave numerous concerts at storied venues and made a few recordings. In the mid-1970s, she seemed to fall off the radar. Some sources reported that she had been diagnosed with cancer as early as 1972.

But in the late 1980s, after she moved to a village outside of Cambridge with her husband, William Barrington-Coupe, a record producer, Hatto began an extraordinary and fertile second summer. With her husband as recording engineer and producer, Hatto began releasing a flood of recordings on her own label, spanning an astonishingly wide swath of repertoire. There were albums of music from Bach , Mozart and Beethoven to Debussy , Prokofiev and Messiaen .

The reviews began trickling in, and they were virtually unanimous in their lavish praise. Richard Dyer, in The Boston Globe , wrote, "Joyce Hatto must be the greatest living pianist that almost no one has ever heard of." She was becoming a cult figure who could do no wrong and whose records were much sought-after and difficult to acquire. When she died in 2006 at age 77, critic Jeremy Nicholas wrote her obituary for The Guardian , stating, "Her legacy is a discography that in quantity, musical range and consistent quality has been equaled by few pianists in history." At that point Hatto had released around 100 albums in a relatively short period.

Less than a year later, the story began to unravel. A curious Gramophone reader contacted the magazine claiming that when he popped his Hatto Liszt recording into his computer, the CD was identified as being performed by the respected Hungarian pianist László Simon. These anomalies quickly multiplied. A Hatto recording of Rachmaninov Piano Concertos registered as Yefim Bronfman's, her album filled with Godowsky was labeled as Carlo Grante's. Nearly all of Hatto's recordings were suddenly suspect.

Gramophone pulled in an audio expert , who compared the soundwaves of Hatto releases and their counterparts by other pianists. Results were "beyond a shadow of a doubt" — they matched. When Barrington-Coupe was questioned about the discrepancies, he doubled down, insisting they were by his wife only.

Finally, in February of 2007, Barrington-Coupe admitted to swapping in other pianists' performances on his wife's albums. Most were stolen whole cloth, and on a few of those he manipulated speeds to disguise the subterfuge. He said he did it for his ailing wife, who tried to legitimately make recordings but couldn't as the cancer sapped her abilities.

Plagiarism is always despicable — and routinely reveals itself in the end. But the Joyce Hatto story is more than just stealing others' work, at least in the eyes of us who write music criticism. It asks questions about jumping on bandwagons, the lines between the objective and the subjective and our perceptions of real and fake. But the critics who fawned over Hatto were not exactly duped, nor did they dupe their readers. What they heard was spectacular playing — just by other pianists, some of whose recordings never enjoyed the rave reviews they got under Hatto's name.

The Hatto affair also serves as a cautionary tale. In today's world of deep fakes and "fake news" and, more to the point, AI technology obfuscating the music industry, Joyce Hatto's grand scandal might appear dangerously quaint. — Tom Huizenga

The picture of a beardless, swagless Rick Ross, smiling in a Miami-Dade County correctional officer's uniform two sizes too tight, became the stuff of rap lore in the summer of 2008. When a photo taken years before he introduced himself to the world as "the biggest Boss" leaked, it challenged the backstory that made him the face of luxury coke rap. His sophomore studio album Trilla — a play on the hip-hop portmanteau for true and real — had just debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 in March. But truth, in this case, required a caveat: Though he took his stage name from one of the most notorious drug kingpins in U.S. history, the man born William Leonard Roberts II had a verifiable history of working for the other side of the law.

In a subgenre full of glorified Stagger Lees, rap was still deeply invested in the perception of authenticity. 50 Cent turned the revelation about Ross into relentless ammo in a beef that nearly amounted to character assassination with diss tracks like "Officer Ricky." He's since admitted to his CO past. But Ross' unmasking didn't undo him. Initially denying the truth, he blamed the photo on "online hackers putting a picture of my face when I was a teenager in high school on other people's body." Then he followed up with 2009's Deeper Than Rap . His third album to debut at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, it solidified his trademark Maybach Music sound. His ability to craft an image was surpassed only by his commitment to songcraft. While detractors like 50 continued to quibble over Ross' questionable background, his growing discography of high-end trap accompanied by lush arrangements and R&B hooks became unimpeachable. Ultimately, Ross beat 50 — and patchworked his own credibility — by making superior art of artifice.

Ross downplays how long he stayed on the prison-guard job to this day (the website The Smoking Gun confirmed it was 18 months.) And 50, for his part, acknowledges his back-and-forth with Ross was always a losing battle. "The most difficult beef to have is when the person you're beefin' with is law enforcement," he said , taking jabs on a recent podcast interview. "When it gets hot, they're just gonna tell." But the biggest win, in hindsight, may have been how Ross' refusal to break character in the moment made us contend with the unfair ways we attribute street rap's gangsta lean to criminality rather than creativity. — Rodney Carmichael

By the time Lana del Rey's debut album Born to Die dropped in 2012, she had already become a lightning rod for critics to argue about the state of authenticity in music. Her retro, hyper-femme look and sex appeal, cribbed from Old Hollywood starlets and recent contemporaries like Amy Winehouse, seemed to eclipse coverage of her actual music. When her single "Video Games," was released on YouTube with a lo-fi video of a then-unsigned del Rey singing the song to her computer camera, it received instant virality and acclaim. Questions about the seemingly DIY start of her music career followed almost immediately.

Critics and armchair commentators quickly became obsessed with poking holes in the story. Lana del Rey, would you believe it, was a stage name — and she had released less successful music before, under her real name, Lizzy Grant. She was also blonde for a period before going brunette as Lana, a clear impossibility, as anyone knows. Her "gangsta Nancy Sinatra" brand — a descriptor bestowed by her label — seemed contradicted by a boarding school upbringing in upstate New York, a reality she did not obscure in interviews. "Who is the real Lizzy Grant/Lana Del Rey?" the highly ironic blog Hipster Runoff posed in an "exposé" at the time, a bombshell investigation that now seems extremely silly.

None of these concerns were lobbed with the same level of disdain at any of del Rey's pop peers at the time, like Lady Gaga, a once aspiring electroclash club artist named Stefanie Germanotta, or Katy Perry, whose debut album was a Christian pop record released under her real name, Katy Hudson. Not to mention a lineage of artists, from Bob Dylan to The White Stripes to Lou Reed, who blurred the lines of their real biographies and fanaticism to create drama or toy with journalists and the listening public.

I suspect that's partly because critics could not make sense of del Rey's slippage between the candied, commercial pop of the 2010s and the raw singer-songwriter streak in her music that's only become more pronounced as her career has continued, an ambiguity listeners are a lot more attuned to now. "Video Games" was beloved by Pitchfork, but the more bubblegum fare on Born to Die was famously hated. Maybe if she had committed to either lane — the scrappy, indie mythos of a group like The White Stripes, or the straight costuming of a Gaga — critics would have calmed down a bit. But even today, with del Rey widely recognized as a truly great, multi-Grammy-nominated songwriter, she's still able to confuse people about what's fake and what's real when it comes to her artistic identity. Moonlighting as a waitress at a Waffle House, marrying a swamp tour guide, spinning in-depth odes to how much she loves making dinner for her husband — these are the stories of a Lana del Rey song, but also just her life. Maybe she was one of the more authentic singers out there from the start. — Hazel Cills

In 2016, when scrolling through the Instagram account of musician and model Miquela Sousa, or as she's better known, Lil Miquela, I stared at a picture of her and tried to figure out if she was a real person. Parts of her image looked real; other aspects looked like a bad Photoshop retouching job, or just plain fake. Whatever it was, Lil Miquela's profile struggled to cross the uncanny valley. As I scoured the Instagram comments and the rest of her pictures, I found I was not alone. There were theories online and arguments that whatever she was, it was unethical.

At that time, with accessible and consumer-forward AI still a couple years away, her creators were able to keep her origins ambiguous. She was positioned as a mysterious, cool girl who made lo-fi, pop and R&B songs. She's attracted millions of followers, posting about being featured on Spotify's "Fresh Finds" playlist, casually posing with musicians like Diplo and Rico Nasty , and even attending the Grammys . Her social media accounts have also reflected what people expect of many musicians and influencers, from posts about her personal life to political stances .

In 2018, Lil Miquela's account officially revealed that she was created by the Los Angeles-based startup Brud (head-spinningly, it did so in the form of a notes app screenshot apology that a human artist might write). The increased prevalence of AI these days has resulted in less ambiguity — as platforms like Instagram and Spotify crack down on AI-generated profiles, both Lil Miquela's Instagram and Spotify profiles make it clear she's an AI persona.

At Lil Miquela's most popular, her fans' attitude was that of any influencer's hive: She was a muse and a fashion icon who lived an enviable life, albeit a fake one. Maybe she benefited from novelty: Now, with the internet flooded with AI-generated content, a digitally rendered person is easy to cast away and ignore. Back in 2016, her followers were quick to let the question of her humanity melt away and accept a fake influencer created by a tech company as the newest route to fame, a spark that ignited the AI-generated reality that consumes online culture today.

item.content:encoded:
From manufactured fans to AI artists and "industry plants," 2026 is one wild year for figuring out what's authentic and what's not in the music industry. For more, check out our historical survey of fakes , a podcast about why it feels harder than ever to know what's real and an essay by Ann Powers on where our desire for authenticity comes from.

Earlier this summer, British producer and singer James Blake posted a series of complaints on his Instagram: He claimed that the music industry is essentially rigged, and that album reviews, comment sections and streaming numbers are all increasingly being manipulated for profit.

"If you're an artist, remember that in 2026 there's not a single part of the system that isn't faked," he wrote.

In a year where an indie darling's success has been called a "psyop" and a pop star's debut album is dogged with plagiarism allegations , Blake raised an interesting point. There's a growing tension between the rise of generative AI, social media algorithms' effect on creative forces and the hypercommercialization of the music industry. Dead internet theory , or the idea that everything online is fake, has taken hold in music; it claims that what was once a human-led space for communication and innovation has turned into a wasteland of bot-programmed activity. At the same time, Gen Z continues to prioritize live music and communal experiences, spending more than ever on concert tickets to do so. Beloved indie stars who had taken a step back from the public eye returned with widely celebrated albums, and streaming services started implementing more and more safeguards around AI content on their platforms.

The year has also had more than its share of bizarre — and dare I say fun? — mysteries that have popped up online: a rabbit hole investigation into the real identity of an underground artist and TikTok song parodies that are somehow on the cutting edge of U.S. immigration law. For better or worse, is 2026 shaping up to be one of the fakest years in music?

Here's a sampling that indicates why the feeling of artifice in music has been so pervasive this year:

In March, the co-founders of a digital marketing agency called Chaotic Good Projects spoke to Billboard during a live podcasting taping at SXSW. During the conversation, they opened up about one of their strategies for manufacturing hype: creating fake fan accounts to post, comment and share videos of the artists on their roster, which ranged from major pop stars to indie rock bands.

The conversation went mostly unnoticed until indie musician Eliza McLamb wrote about it on her Substack. She expressed surprise not at the existence of online narrative campaigns, which are a continuation of decades-old marketing tactics, but at the irony of smaller, alternative artists like Cameron Winter and Oklou being beneficiaries of Chaotic Good's mainstream virality machine. (Chaotic Good changed elements of its website and took down its roster shortly after McLamb's piece was published; the agency has not responded to NPR's past requests for comment.) The controversy snowballed when WIRED picked up the story, writing an article about Winter's band — which had recently released its breakthrough album, Getting Killed , and was in the midst of enormous critical acclaim — titled " The Fanfare Around the Band Geese is a Psyop ."

In an interview with Rolling Stone months later, Geese frontman Cameron Winter said the band had been just as taken aback by the viral story and the band's seemingly overnight explosion. "We were just like, 'Oh, my God. The whole f***ing thing is fake.' We were having a meltdown," Winter said. "Then we marched up to our label over email, the relevant team members, like, 'How long have all our f***ing fans been fake, you sons of b******?'"

According to Winter, the label explained they had hired Chaotic Good to repost clips of the band's performances and help push it onto algorithms, not to create fake fan accounts or flood comments with bots. Even so, the Chaotic Good discourse sowed distrust around artists who seem to suddenly go viral and in the authenticity of their fandoms. (For what it's worth, Geese has been playing festivals and selling out its biggest headlining tour for all of 2026, and the people in the mosh pits look pretty real).

When Harry Styles announced his 30-night residency at Madison Square Garden at the beginning of the year, tickets sold out almost immediately — kind of.

In April, Ticketmaster announced it had identified and canceled thousands of tickets that had been purchased by scalpers, who the company claimed used fake identities to create multiple accounts and bypass ticket limits. Saumil Mehta, global president of Ticketmaster, wrote in a statement that the tickets would be sold back to real fans at face value.

The announcement followed years of debate about how Ticketmaster prices concert tickets , how it manages virtual queues for high-demand shows, and how it does (or doesn't) restrict the resale market . It also coincided with the end of a high-profile antitrust trial involving Ticketmaster and its parent company, Live Nation, and dozens of states who accused the conglomerate of exercising too much power over too many aspects of the live music industry — including by overcharging fans.

Producer and musician Jack Antonoff responded to Ticketmaster's statement about catching scalpers on X with sarcasm: "you caught you?"

Last year, a long-haired, bell-bottom-wearing character named Mr. Fantasy started making waves on TikTok, releasing a string of electropop songs with goofy videos. Social media users soon started pointing out the physical resemblance between the eccentric singer and the Riverdale actor KJ Apa, including the fact that they seemingly have the same tattoos. When asked about his identity in interviews, Mr. Fantasy cheekily denied any relation to Apa. In a statement to NPR last year, Mr. Fantasy's manager claimed to not know who "that TJ Apple actor boy is."

In May of this year, Mr. Fantasy upped the ante when he released a music video featuring several of Apa's Riverdale costars. KJ Apa then posted a now-deleted video on Instagram, alluding to the singer and accusing him of having "completely and utterly stolen my identity and likeness," and adding that it was costing him acting jobs. Mr. Fantasy later told Entertainment Tonight that he and Kapa had "talked it out."

"What a drag it is getting old," Mick Jagger crooned in 1966. If only he knew that 60 years later, he would be able to de-age himself — at least for a few minutes.

This summer, The Rolling Stones released the single "In the Stars" ahead of the group's 25th studio album, Foreign Tongues . In the music video, Jagger, Keith Richards and Ronnie Wood appear as younger versions of themselves, playing an impromptu show in a warehouse party alongside rising actress Odessa A'Zion. The deepfake versions of the Stones were created by Deep Voodoo, an AI startup formed by South Park creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone.

Despite originally being released in 2024, indie pop singer Malcolm Todd's song "Earrings" has spent much of 2026 climbing the Billboard Hot 100 chart — a trajectory that has become more and more common thanks to how TikTok boosts songs into virality.

The song has seen a surge in streams, too. In June, "Earrings" spiked in listenership by 70% overnight, landing it at the top of the Spotify USA charts. The Financial Times reported that the song's meteoric rise coincided with bets on the prediction market Kalshi that it would be the most-streamed song in June; Spotify later deleted more than half a million streams on "Earrings" after it determined that the song's numbers had been manipulated by bots.

In a statement shared with NPR, Spotify said, "All streaming services face ever-changing stream manipulation. Spotify has best-in-class detection and mitigation practices for manipulated streams, and we don't pay out associated royalties."

Representatives for Todd did not respond to NPR's request for comment.

This summer, music streaming company Deezer reported that for the first time ever, AI-generated songs constituted more than 50% of its daily uploads in the month of June. But the songs accounted for less than 3% of total streams on the platform, and a majority of those streams were deemed fraudulent, meaning they're likely driven by bots rather than human listeners.

Deezer's announcement came soon after a report published by the entertainment insights company Luminate, which found that although generative AI content is flooding streaming platforms, listeners are becoming less and less comfortable with it.

Over the last few years, Gracie Abrams has become one of the most popular confessional singer-songwriters of her generation. The 27-year-old has opened for Taylor Swift, been mentored by indie rock veteran and frequent collaborator Aaron Dessner and is now headlining arena shows. But because she is the daughter of filmmaker J.J. Abrams and Hollywood producer Katie McGrath, Abrams is often accused of being a "nepo baby." That term, which has become almost inescapable on the internet, basically accuses a person with influential parents of climbing the music (or other) industry via connections driven by nepotism rather than talent, hard work or real popularity.

The term is used widely to describe almost any star who could have had a leg up thanks to their family connections (see also Sombr, Clairo or Stella Lefty), but it's been a particularly pervasive line of questioning for Abrams this year, as she was on the press tour for her album Daughter From Hell in July. During an interview with The New York Times ' Popcast , Abrams acknowledged the debate around the term.

"The nepo stuff is obviously in the discourse appropriately," she said. "I think about the privilege there, and it's like, I had a safety net, and that allowed me the ability to experiment and to concentrate and I had the gift of time to dedicate to doing this thing I loved. I wasn't growing up afraid financially, and that's the biggest deal."

Daughter From Hell , which largely contends with Abrams' coming-of-age and her relationship to her mother, was the singer's first album to debut at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart. Most major stops of her upcoming tour to promote the album are sold out.

With a decline in traditional media and arts journalism in particular, there's been a rise in a new medium for music discovery: short-form video content that recommends, analyzes and dissects new songs. The influencers who run these accounts have become the modern-day equivalent to VJs; they're increasingly popular as music fans face algorithmic fatigue and look for trusted voices to put them on.

But it turns out that some of these videos, which usually look like organic fan content, are a form of paid advertising. Over the summer, NPR spoke with five music content creators who said they often accept payments from record labels and marketing agencies to promote certain songs — and they don't disclose any type of sponsorship in their posts.
